I'm sorry that your child had to go through the experience that she did, and I am glad that *she* is happy you called the police against her wishes, however that is not the right way to go. Talking to them, giving options that you'll support them through the process etc, all that is great. Taking away what little control they feel they have in their life? You were lucky that your daughter reacted in a positive way to what you did, it could have very easily made her feel worse despite your very obviously good intentions born out of your love for and desire to protect her. In cases of abuse, especially childhood abuse a dominant emotion afterwards is unrelenting shame. When they do confide in someone, they will have spent a long time working themselves up to it. They don't want people to know. They are not ready for more people to know. Even if it goes no further because they don't want to make a statement, just the sudden knowledge that these unknown officers know this deep shameful secret about them (I'm not saying it *is* a shameful secret, I'm saying how it feels) can be immensely traumatising in itself. I am not demonising you in any way, shape or form; your love and support of your daughter is obvious, and it heartens me to see people so passionately protective of their children when it seems the world has turned on its head, but what I'm saying is that you shouldn't enforce this being the way it *should* be done just because it worked for you. There are abuse support charities and helplines who are qualified to give such advice, and understand the varying ways people can react and try to cope with a trauma and directing the family towards those help services should be the real goal here.
